milestone.title: Rite of Acceptance
milestone.about: You stand at the church door and are welcomed in front of the parish. You become a catechumen (or, if already baptized, a candidate).

stages.title: Catechumenate
stages.subtitle: Learning the faith with Symbolon, week by week

milestone.title: Rite of Election
milestone.about: Usually on the first Sunday of Lent, with the bishop. Your name is written in the Book of the Elect: the Church chooses you for the sacraments at Easter.

milestone.title: Easter Vigil
milestone.about: The night before Easter. You receive baptism (if not yet baptized), confirmation, and your first Communion.

sessions.title: Welcome: the road to Emmaus
sessions.summary: Every journey of faith starts with Jesus walking beside us, often before we recognize him.
lesson: On the first Easter Sunday, two disciples walked home from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles away. They were sad and confused: Jesus had died, and they did not understand the news that he was alive.

A stranger joined them on the road. He listened to them, then explained the Scriptures, showing how everything pointed to Jesus. When they reached the village they begged him, "Stay with us." At supper he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them. Their eyes were opened: it was Jesus.

Later they said to each other, "Were not our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us on the way?" That is the heart of this journey. You will hear the Scriptures, ask questions, walk with others, and come to the table of the Eucharist. Jesus is already walking with you, even on the days you do not see him.
You do not need to have everything figured out. The disciples on the road were full of doubts. Bring your questions; that is what this time is for.
sessions.reflection: What brought you to begin this journey? What are you hoping to find?

sessions.title: Prayer: talking with God
sessions.summary: Prayer is simply a conversation with God who loves you. Anyone can start today.
lesson: Prayer is lifting your heart and mind to God. It does not need special words; you can talk to God as you would to someone who loves you. Saint Thérèse of Lisieux called prayer "a surge of the heart, a simple look turned toward heaven."

Catholics pray in many ways: in our own words, with traditional prayers like the Our Father, with the Bible, in silence, and together at Mass. Traditional prayers are helpful when we do not know what to say; they have been prayed by millions of people before us.
When the disciples asked Jesus, "Lord, teach us to pray," he gave them the Our Father. It is the perfect place to start. Try praying it slowly once a day this week, thinking about each line.

A simple daily habit: when you wake up, make the Sign of the Cross and offer your day to God. Before sleep, think back over the day, thank God for one good thing, and say sorry for anything you regret.
sessions.reflection: What would help you make a few minutes of prayer part of your day?

sessions.title: The journey of faith: the Trinity, faith, and the God who is love
sessions.summary: God made us out of love, to share his life. He has shown us who he is: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

sources.title: Psalm 23, The Lord is my shepherd

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 1
lesson: This session opens with Psalm 23, "The Lord is my shepherd," alongside a picture of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus. Both say the same thing: we are not walking alone. God goes ahead of us, walks beside us, and leads us home.
[[art:Angelsatmamre-trinity-rublev-1410.jpg|Andrei Rublev, The Trinity (about 1410): the three visitors to Abraham, an image of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit]]
## Made by love, for love
God did not need to create us. He is perfectly happy and complete in himself. He made us freely, out of pure goodness, so that we could share in his own blessed life (Catechism 1, 293).
That is why every human heart carries a longing that nothing in this world fully satisfies. We were made by the God who is love, and we are made for his love (Catechism 27-30).
> Our hearts are restless until they rest in you. — St. Augustine

And God is not waiting for us to find our own way to him. At every moment of our lives he comes close, calling us to seek him, to know him and to love him (Catechism 1). Like the shepherd of Psalm 23, he is the one who comes looking for us.
## One God, three Persons

There is only one God (Catechism 200-202). Yet God has revealed that his one life is a communion of three Persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Catechism 221). We could never have worked this out on our own. We know it because God showed us, by sending his Son, Jesus, and then his Holy Spirit.

This is God's "inmost secret": his very being is love shared between Persons. As the Catechism says, God himself is an eternal exchange of love, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and he has made us to share in that exchange (Catechism 221).

The diagram below, sometimes called the Shield of the Trinity, helps keep this straight. Each Person is fully God. But the Persons are truly distinct: the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is not the Father.
[[figure:trinity]]

So we must avoid two mistakes. It is not three gods working together, and it is not one God simply wearing three masks. The Church worships one God in the Trinity, without mixing up the Persons or dividing God's one being. Their glory is equal and their majesty is eternal (Catechism 266).
## What faith is
Faith is our answer to the God who has made himself known. It has two sides (Catechism 150).
- Intellect: with our minds we believe, saying yes to what God has revealed.
- Will: with our hearts we choose to entrust our whole lives to him, the way you would trust a friend with everything.
[[figure:faith]]
Faith is not only agreeing with ideas, and it is not only a feeling. It is both: knowing who God is, and choosing to lean on him.
## Three key elements of prayer
Prayer is how faith becomes a relationship. Three simple elements can shape it:
- Praise: start by focusing on God, not on your problems. This is the "truth zone": God is in control and he loves you. Tell him you love him too.
- Petition: ask for what you and others need. Nothing is too small to bring to him.
- Forgiveness: ask God to forgive your sins, and choose to forgive the people who have hurt you.

> We must speak to God as a friend speaks to his friend, as a servant to his master; now asking some favor, now acknowledging our faults, and communicating to him all that concerns us: our thoughts, our fears, our projects, our desires, and in all things seeking his counsel. — St. Ignatius of Loyola
sessions.reflection: Pray Psalm 23 slowly this week. Where in your life do you need to trust that God is the shepherd walking with you?

deeper.title: Why two creeds?
deeper.text:
A creed is a short summary of what Christians believe. The Church keeps two from the early centuries, and both proclaim faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

The Apostles' Creed is one of the earliest, first used in Rome when people were baptized. We still use it at Baptisms and to begin the Rosary.

The Nicene Creed was first written at the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD to answer questions that had arisen about the Trinity and about whether Jesus is truly God. Its extra detail is about clarity. It is the creed we normally say at Sunday Mass and on major feasts.

sessions.title: Divine Revelation: God seeking us
sessions.summary: God has shown us who he is and his loving plan to save us. It reaches us through Scripture, Tradition and the Church's teaching, all three together.

sources.title: Matthew 16:13-19, the keys of the kingdom
John 16:12-15, the Spirit will guide you into all truth
Dei Verbum (Vatican II on Divine Revelation)
Catechism 50-100: God comes to meet us

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 2
lesson: Session 2 opens with a famous painting by Perugino in the Sistine Chapel: Jesus handing the keys of the kingdom to Peter, the first pope (Matthew 16:18-19). Hold on to that picture. It shows how God makes sure what he revealed is handed on faithfully.
[[art:Rembrandt Harmensz van Rijn - Return of the Prodigal Son - Google Art Project.jpg|Rembrandt, The Return of the Prodigal Son (about 1668): the Father who comes looking for us]]
## God shows himself

"Divine Revelation" means God making himself known. We could never reach God by our own effort alone, so he chose to reveal himself and his loving plan to save us, so that we could know him and love him (Catechism 50-52).

He did this step by step, through deeds and words, across a long story: creation, Abraham, Moses, the kings and prophets of Israel. This story of God gradually saving his people is called salvation history (Catechism 53-64).

That story reaches its high point in Jesus Christ, the Son of God made man. He is not just one more messenger. He is the fullness of Revelation: in him God has said everything he wanted to say (Catechism 65). That is why the Church teaches that no new public revelation is coming before Jesus returns.
## How it reaches us: Scripture and Tradition
Jesus did not hand his apostles a finished book. He taught them, lived with them, and sent them out to preach. What he revealed was passed on in two ways (Catechism 75-79):
- Sacred Tradition: the living handing-on, first by word of mouth, of everything Christ did and taught, through the Church's teaching, life and worship (Catechism 76-78).
- Sacred Scripture: the part of that same Revelation the Holy Spirit inspired to be written down, the Bible (Catechism 81).

They are not two competing sources but one stream flowing from the same spring. Nothing in Tradition can contradict Scripture, and Scripture is best understood in the light of the Tradition it came from (Catechism 80-83).
## Who interprets it: the Magisterium

The apostles entrusted this whole "deposit of faith" to the Church. The Magisterium (from the Latin for "teacher") is the teaching office of the Church: the pope and the bishops in communion with him, the successors of Peter and the apostles. Its job is to interpret God's word faithfully, not to add to it (Catechism 84-86). It serves the word of God; it is not above it.
That is what the keys in the painting mean. Jesus gave Peter real authority so that his followers in every century could know they are hearing the true faith and not just someone's opinion.
## The three-legged stool
Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium work together. Take away any one, and the whole thing topples (Catechism 95).
[[figure:stool]]
> Sacred Tradition, Sacred Scripture and the teaching authority of the Church are so linked and joined together that one cannot stand without the others. — Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum 10
## Complete, yet still unfolding

If everything has been revealed in Jesus, is there anything left to learn? Yes. Jesus promised that the Holy Spirit would guide his Church into all truth (John 16:13). Revelation is complete, but the Church keeps understanding it more deeply over the centuries (Catechism 66).

One writer compares it to a flower: Christ gave the apostles the whole bud, and over the centuries its petals keep opening, bringing more light. Nothing new is added; what was there all along is seen more clearly.
## Hear it and live it
> Be doers of the word and not hearers only, deluding yourselves. — James 1:22
St. James says that hearing God's word and walking away unchanged is like looking in a mirror and forgetting your own face. God reveals himself so that we can live differently.

And this is freedom. Freedom is not doing whatever you want; it is being able to do what is truly good. God is a loving Father who knows what is best for us, and through Revelation the Church has been given the tools to live in true freedom. The goal is to share eternal life with God and our heavenly family. We do not walk alone: the Church on earth and in heaven helps us along the way.

deeper.title: Two words worth knowing
deeper.text:
Salvation history is the story of everything God has done to rescue and draw humanity back to himself: from creation, through Abraham, Moses and the prophets, to Jesus, and on through the Church until he comes again. The Bible is, at heart, this one long story.

Magisterium is the Church's teaching office: the pope and the bishops united with him. When it teaches on faith and morals, it is guarding and explaining what God has already revealed in Scripture and Tradition, never inventing something new.

sessions.reflection: Is there a part of God's word you have heard but not yet put into practice? What is one small step you could take this week?

sessions.title: The Bible: God's love letter
sessions.summary: The Bible is God's love letter to his children: inspired by the Holy Spirit, read with the Church, and meant to be prayed.

sources.title: Dei Verbum (Vatican II on Divine Revelation)

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 3
lesson: The Bible is not a dry history book or a collection of moral fables where the good guy always wins. It is the story of a God who comes looking for the lost and saves them at great cost to himself. Think of it as a long love letter from a Father to his children who are still on the road home.
[[art:Saint Jerome Writing-Caravaggio (1605-6).jpg|Caravaggio, Saint Jerome Writing (about 1606): Jerome translated the Bible into Latin]]
## Inspired by the Holy Spirit
- The Word of God in human words: Scripture is God speaking to us through the language of people (Catechism 101).

- Two authors at once: God is the author of Scripture. He inspired human writers who were real authors too, using their own language, style and abilities, yet they wrote what God wanted written, and nothing more (Catechism 105-106).
- Always true: because the Holy Spirit stands behind what the human authors affirm, Scripture teaches faithfully and without error the truth God wanted written for our salvation (Catechism 107).
## Reading it the Catholic way

Catholics do not read the Bible literalistically, as if every sentence were a newspaper report. We read it literarily: paying attention to what each human author meant to say, and to what God wants to reveal through them (Catechism 109-114).

That means asking about the time and culture it was written in, and the kind of writing it is. The Bible contains history, prophecy, poetry, law, letters and more, and each tells the truth in its own way (Catechism 110). A psalm is read like a song, not like a legal document.
## The four senses of Scripture
An ancient tradition sees two main levels of meaning in Scripture: the literal and the spiritual. The spiritual sense has three parts (Catechism 115-118).
- Literal: what the words actually mean, found through careful study. Every other sense is built on this one.
- Allegorical: how events point to Christ. For example, Israel crossing the Red Sea is a sign of Baptism.
- Moral: how the text teaches us to live justly. St. Paul says these things were written "for our instruction" (1 Corinthians 10:11).
- Anagogical: from a Greek word meaning "leading up." How events point to our eternal destiny. Jerusalem, for example, points to the heavenly city.
> The Letter speaks of deeds; Allegory to faith; The Moral how to act; Anagogy our destiny. — Medieval saying, quoted in the Catechism 118
## Which books belong: the canon
All of Scripture tells one story, the story of salvation that reaches its climax in Jesus. The Old Testament prepares for the New, and the New fulfills the Old (Catechism 121-123, 128-129).

Guided by the Holy Spirit through apostolic Tradition, the Church discerned which books belong in the Bible. That complete list is called the canon (Catechism 120): 46 books in the Old Testament and 27 in the New, 73 in all.
[[figure:canon]]

Most Protestant Bibles have 66 books. During the Reformation, Martin Luther moved seven Old Testament books into a separate section, and later Protestant Bibles dropped them: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and 1 and 2 Maccabees, along with parts of Esther and Daniel. Catholics call these the deuterocanonical books. They were in the Greek Old Testament used by the early Christians, and the Church has always counted them as Scripture.
## How to start reading and praying the Bible
The Church has always seen Scripture as food for Christian life (Catechism 131). St. Jerome put it bluntly: "Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ" (Catechism 133).
> The Holy Bible is like a mirror before our mind's eye. In it we see our inner face. — Pope St. Gregory the Great

- Start with Sunday: you already hear Scripture at every Mass. Read the Sunday readings ahead of time. Magazines and apps like The Word Among Us and Magnificat give each day's readings with a short meditation and prayer.
- Make it part of daily prayer: read one of the Gospels, a chapter or even a few verses a day. The Psalms are great for prayer too; many are prayers of King David, written in good times and bad.
- Just begin: God speaks to you personally through Scripture. Even one line can bring insight or comfort. The Word of God is for everyone, so do not worry about how much you know.
Mother Angelica, the American nun who founded EWTN, used to say that the Gospel is not only a record of the past: it is a guide for living today, so we read it to put it into practice.

deeper.title: Covenant: the thread through the whole Bible
deeper.text:
A covenant is a sacred bond. A contract exchanges property and makes promises; a covenant exchanges persons and is sealed with a solemn oath, making people family. That is why Scripture is better read as a family story than a courtroom drama: God is a Father, not just a judge.

All through the Old Testament, God makes covenants with his people, and each one widens his family: a couple (Adam), a household (Noah), a tribe (Abraham), a nation (Moses), a kingdom (David). Again and again the people break their side of the covenant, and they suffer the consequences.

Jesus establishes the New Covenant. He keeps it perfectly, takes on himself the curse of our broken promises, and opens God's family to the whole world. He is the one mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5), and the sign of this covenant is the Eucharist: "This cup is the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20).

[[figure:covenants]]

sessions.reflection: Choose one Gospel and read a few verses each day this week. Which line stayed with you, and why?

sessions.title: The story of salvation: creation, fall, and redemption
sessions.summary: The whole Bible in three words: Creation, Fall, Redemption. God made us one family, sin broke it, and Jesus gathers us home.

sources.title: Genesis 12:1-3 and 22:15-18: God's promises to Abraham
Pope Benedict XVI, homily at the start of his pontificate (2005)

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 4
lesson: Every good story has a beginning, a crisis and a rescue. The Bible is the greatest of them, and it is true: it is the story of God and of us. Its shape fits in three words: Creation, Fall and Redemption. Once you see this shape, every part of Scripture finds its place.
[[art:Michelangelo - Creation of Adam (cropped).jpg|Michelangelo, The Creation of Adam (about 1512), Sistine Chapel, Vatican]]
[[figure:salvation]]
## Creation: made for love

God is perfectly happy in himself. He did not need us. He made us freely, out of sheer goodness, so that we could share his own blessed life (Catechism 1). We were made to know him, to love him and to live with him forever.
> Each of us is the result of a thought of God. Each of us is willed, each of us is loved, each of us is necessary. — Pope Benedict XVI

In the beginning everything was in harmony: the first man and woman were at peace with God, with each other, with themselves and with creation (Catechism 374-376). Think of two lines: a vertical line joining us to God, and a horizontal line joining us to one another. In creation both were whole.
## The Fall: love refused

God gave Adam and Eve real freedom, because love that is forced is not love. Tempted by the devil, they stopped trusting God and chose themselves instead of him (Catechism 396-398). They refused the self-giving love they were made for.

Both lines broke at once. The vertical bond with God was cut, and the horizontal bond between people cracked too: Adam blames Eve, Cain kills Abel, and the family of God scatters (Catechism 400). The Church calls this wound original sin.
- Original sin: not a sin we committed, but a wounded human nature we inherited. We are born without the holiness and friendship with God that we were meant to have (Catechism 404-405).
- Concupiscence: the pull toward sin that remains even after Baptism washes original sin away. It is not itself a sin, but it makes the good harder to choose (Catechism 405, 1264).
## Redemption: God comes to rescue
God did not give up on us. Right after the Fall he promised a Savior (Genesis 3:15). Then, step by step, through covenants, he began gathering his scattered family again.
God made three great promises to Abraham, and the rest of the Old Testament shows him keeping them:
- A great nation: fulfilled when God freed Israel from Egypt through Moses and made them his people at Sinai.
- A kingdom: fulfilled when God made David king and promised that his throne would last forever.
- A blessing for every nation: fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David, who opens God's family to the whole world in the new and everlasting covenant.

In Jesus all three lines meet. The Son of God became man to reconcile us with God, to show us God's love, to be our model of holiness and to make us sharers in God's own life (Catechism 457-460). He paid the debt of sin we could not pay, and the Holy Spirit now fills those who believe.
## The Church: God's family gathered

Jesus did not leave us as scattered individuals. He founded the Church to gather the broken human family into one family of God, a sign and instrument of our union with God and with each other (Catechism 775-776). That is what "catholic" means: universal, sent to everyone (Catechism 830-831).

Before ascending, Jesus gave the apostles a mission: proclaim the Gospel, baptize, and make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19-20; Catechism 849). The Church has carried that mission ever since, passing on his teaching and the grace of the sacraments, and will until he comes again.
## Where we fit in the story

This story is still being written, and we are in it. Every day we choose between good and evil, light and darkness. The devil rarely tempts us with something obviously evil. More often he keeps us busy, distracted and amused, living only for the world so that we never stop to ask what we were made for.
The way out is simple, though not always easy: turn toward the light of Christ, again and again. Each small choice for God is a step back into the family we were made for.

deeper.title: Why the story matters
deeper.text:
Without Creation, we would not know we are loved and made on purpose. Without the Fall, we could not explain why the world, and our own hearts, are so mixed up. Without Redemption, there would be no hope.

People sometimes call the Bible's story the greatest story ever told. It is better than a story, because it is true: God wrote himself into history to bring his children home.

- Catholic: from the Greek kath' holou, "according to the whole": the Church is for every people, place and time (Catechism 830-831).

- Redemption: buying back. Jesus paid the price of our freedom with his own life (Mark 10:45).

sessions.reflection: Where do you see the "broken lines" in your own life, with God or with the people around you? What is one small step toward the light this week?

sessions.title: Who is Jesus?
sessions.summary: Jesus is truly God and truly man: one divine Person with two natures. The Church guarded this truth against every distortion, because our salvation depends on it.

sources.title: John 14:1-14: the way, the truth and the life
Hebrews 1:1-4: God has spoken through his Son
Pope St. John Paul II, World Youth Day vigil, Rome (2000)

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 5
lesson: > It is Jesus that you seek when you dream of happiness; he is waiting for you when nothing else you find satisfies you. — Pope St. John Paul II, World Youth Day 2000
[[art:Spas vsederzhitel sinay.jpg|Christ Pantocrator (6th century), St. Catherine's Monastery, Sinai: one face, truly God and truly man]]

Every person eventually has to answer the question Jesus asked his disciples: "Who do you say that I am?" (Matthew 16:15). Christianity is not first a set of rules or ideas. It is a relationship with a Person.
## God's final Word

For centuries God spoke to his people in many ways through the prophets. In Jesus he spoke his whole Word at once (Hebrews 1:1-2). St. John of the Cross put it beautifully: in giving us his Son, God told us everything, and he has nothing more to say (Catechism 65).
- No new public revelation: we do not wait for a new gospel. The Church spends the centuries understanding more deeply what Jesus has already given (Catechism 66).

- Private revelations: some, like Fatima or Lourdes, are approved by the Church. They do not add to the faith; they help people live it in a certain time. No Catholic is required to believe them (Catechism 67).
- For everyone: God wants all people to be saved and to come to know the truth (1 Timothy 2:4; Catechism 74).
## True God and true man

The Son of God did not stop being God when he became man, and he did not just look human. He became truly one of us while remaining truly God. This is the Incarnation: God taking on flesh (Catechism 464).
[[figure:natures]]

Jesus is one Person, the eternal Son, with two natures, divine and human. They are united without being mixed together and without being split apart. As man he had a real body, a human soul, a human mind that learned, and a human will that freely obeyed the Father (Catechism 470-475, 479-483). He got tired, wept, and felt joy and fear. He is like us in all things but sin (Hebrews 4:15).
## Why the Church guarded every word

In the first centuries, many people tried to make Jesus easier to understand by trimming away part of the mystery. Each attempt ended up with a Jesus who could not save us. The Church's great councils answered them, and that is where the precise words of our Creed come from.

- Arianism (4th century): taught that the Son was a creature, the first and greatest, but not God. The Council of Nicaea (325) answered that he is "begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father" (Catechism 465).
- Adoptionism (3rd century): taught that Jesus was an ordinary man whom God adopted as his Son at his baptism.
- Docetism and Gnosticism: taught that Jesus only seemed to have a body (from the Greek dokein, "to seem") and only seemed to suffer.
- Apollinarianism (4th century): taught that the divine Word took the place of a human mind in Jesus, so he was not fully human.

- Nestorianism: split Christ into two persons, a human one and a divine one, and so would not call Mary the Mother of God. The Council of Ephesus (431) answered that Mary is Theotokos, the God-bearer, because her Son is one divine Person (Catechism 466).
- Monophysitism: taught that the human nature dissolved into the divine, like a drop of water in the sea. The Council of Chalcedon (451) answered: two natures, one Person (Catechism 467).
## Why it matters

This is not word-games. If Jesus were not truly God, his death could not reconcile us with God. If he were not truly man, he could not stand in our place, and our humanity would not be healed. The early bishop St. Gregory of Nazianzus summed it up: what was not taken up by Christ was not redeemed.
## Lord, liar, or something worse?

Jesus forgave sins, claimed to be one with the Father, and accepted worship. The writer C.S. Lewis pointed out that someone who said such things could not be merely a fine moral teacher. Either he was lying, or he was badly deluded, or he was telling the truth and is Lord. The one option he did not leave open is the polite one in the middle.
Jesus answers the question himself: "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6).
## Meeting him

Archbishop Fulton Sheen, the much-loved TV bishop, made an hour of prayer before the Blessed Sacrament every day of his priesthood. He said it was what kept him breathing spiritually, like an oxygen tank. Knowing about Jesus is a start; the goal is to know him, personally, in prayer, Scripture and the sacraments.

deeper.title: Words the Church uses for Jesus
deeper.text:
- Incarnation: from the Latin for "in the flesh." The Son of God became man in the womb of the Virgin Mary (John 1:14).

- Hypostatic union: the theologian's name for two natures united in one divine Person.

- Consubstantial: of the same substance. We say it in the Creed: the Son is God in exactly the same way the Father is.

- Theotokos: Greek for God-bearer. Calling Mary the Mother of God is really a statement about who Jesus is.

- Christ: Greek for Messiah, "the anointed one." It is a title, not a surname.

sessions.reflection: Jesus asks you, not just the apostles: "Who do you say that I am?" How would you answer today? Try spending fifteen quiet minutes with him this week, in a church if you can.

sessions.title: The Paschal Mystery
sessions.summary: The Paschal Mystery is Jesus' passion, death, resurrection and ascension: how he restored our friendship with God, and how he invites us to share in it.

sources.title: 1 Peter 3:18-19 and 4:6: preaching to the dead

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 6
lesson: The Paschal Mystery is the mystery of Jesus' death and resurrection. It is the center of the whole faith: everything before it points toward it, and everything after it flows from it.
[[art:Cristo crucificado.jpg|Diego Velázquez, Christ Crucified (about 1632), Prado Museum, Madrid]]
## The cross was shocking

We see crosses everywhere, on walls, steeples and necklaces, so it is easy to forget what one meant in Jesus' day. Crucifixion was the cruelest and most shameful execution Rome had. A Roman wearing a cross as jewelry would have seemed as strange to his neighbors as someone today wearing a tiny electric chair. Yet the cross became the sign of our faith, because on it Jesus won our salvation.
## Why "Paschal"?

Pascha is the Greek form of the Hebrew word for Passover. At the first Passover the blood of a lamb saved Israel's firstborn, and God led his people out of slavery in Egypt. Jesus is the new Passover Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7). By his passion, death, resurrection and ascension, he leads us out of slavery to sin and death (Catechism 571).

We proclaim this at every Mass: "We proclaim your Death, O Lord, and profess your Resurrection until you come again." Beneath it all is one simple reality: Jesus gave himself completely to the Father, out of love, on our behalf.
## Why did Jesus die for our sins?
[[figure:bridge]]
- A real gap: sin is not a small mistake. It broke our friendship with God, the very source of life.
- We cannot bridge it ourselves: God is infinite, and an offense against infinite love leaves a gap no human effort can close. Only an act of infinite worth could repair it.

- God became man to bridge it: as man, Jesus could stand in our place and offer his life for us. As God, his offering had infinite worth. He took our sins on himself freely, as the true sacrifice that the Old Testament sacrifices only foreshadowed (Catechism 613-616).
No one took Jesus' life from him; he laid it down freely (John 10:18). The cross is not a picture of an angry God, but of a love that would go all the way for us.
## He descended to the dead
In the Creed we say Jesus "descended into hell." This does not mean the hell of the damned. It means the realm of the dead, which the Hebrews called Sheol and the Greeks Hades (Catechism 633).

Before Christ, all who died, good and bad, were without the vision of God, waiting for the Messiah. Jesus, his human soul still united to his divine Person, went down to them. He did not go to free the damned or destroy the hell of damnation, but to open heaven to the just who had gone before him (Catechism 632-637). On Holy Saturday his saving work reached every human being of every time and place, back to Adam and Eve.
## He rose from the dead

On the third day Jesus rose, truly and bodily. The tomb was empty, and he ate and spoke with his disciples, who were willing to die rather than deny it. St. Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, our faith is in vain (1 Corinthians 15:14).

By his death Jesus frees us from sin; by his resurrection he opens for us the way to a new life as sons and daughters of God (Catechism 654). He has raised us to new life now, and he has opened the doors of heaven: eternal life with God and with all who have gone before us.
## Sharing in his cross

Jesus invites us into his death and resurrection. We can unite our whole lives with his cross: our daily work, our joys and our sufferings (Catechism 618). The cross and resurrection are the center of history, and they are meant to be the center of each of our lives too.
Everyone suffers sometime; no one avoids it. So the real question is not "Will I suffer?" but "What will I do when I suffer?"
- True love is always sacrificial: it is selfless and turned toward God and others.
- Living only for yourself shrinks you: it makes us selfish, and blind to our own mortality and our true purpose.
- Suffering can be offered: our pain becomes a chance to unite ourselves with the suffering of Jesus, and to offer it for others (Colossians 1:24). Catholics sometimes call this "offering it up."
> In the evening of this life, I shall appear before you with empty hands, for I do not ask you, Lord, to count my works. — St. Thérèse of Lisieux

St. Thérèse loved this image of empty hands. We come to the cross with nothing of our own to boast of, and there the empty are filled: Christ's hands, emptied for us, pour out mercy, and our hands, emptied for him and for others, are filled with his love.

deeper.title: The Triduum: three days at the heart of the year
deeper.text:
The Paschal Mystery is celebrated every Sunday, and above all in the Easter Triduum, the three holiest days of the Church year.

- Holy Thursday: the Mass of the Lord's Supper, when Jesus gives us the Eucharist and the priesthood, and washes his disciples' feet.

- Good Friday: the Celebration of the Lord's Passion. There is no Mass; we venerate the cross.

- Holy Saturday and the Easter Vigil: the Church waits at the tomb, then lights the new fire and sings the Exsultet. At the Vigil, those finishing RCIA are baptized, confirmed and receive their First Communion.

The Paschal Mystery is where your own journey is heading.
